title: The Angels Hurried Lot — Gate, Urging, a Pillar of Salt
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace to you. Last lesson we stood with Abraham on the mountain and heard him pray his way down from fifty righteous men to ten. And then the text says, "Yahweh went his way as soon as he had finished communing with Abraham, and Abraham returned to his place."

Today the camera turns away from the mountain and down to the city on the plain. And before we read a single verse I want to say something important: this is the chapter in the whole of Genesis that is most easily picked up and used as a weapon. So we are going to read it with particular care, and with particular honesty.

And the question this lesson puts to us may already be lodged somewhere inside you: is there something in your life that you know in your heart is wrong, something you are genuinely grieved about — and yet you cannot leave it?

Let me put the answer at the front. The reason any of us is saved has never been that we were the clear-headed ones. It is that a pair of hands could not bear to let us go. And yet — being saved is free, and delay has a price.
1. He Sat in the Gate of the City
Verse 1: "The two angels came to Sodom at evening. Lot sat in the gate of Sodom."
Brothers and sisters, notice two things before anything else.

First, the chapter before had "three men"; this chapter has only "two angels." The third one stayed behind, standing in front of Abraham, and it was with him that Abraham held that long conversation of intercession. The writer has counted heads very carefully.
Second, and this one matters more: "Lot sat in the gate of Sodom."

In the ancient Near East the city gate was not simply a door. It was a plaza — the place where the elders sat in council, where cases were tried, where business was done. To sit in the gate means that this man already held a position of standing in that city.

Now trace his route again. Genesis 13:10 — he "lifted up his eyes, and saw all the plain of the Jordan." Genesis 13:12 — he "moved his tent as far as Sodom." Genesis 14:12 — he is the man "who lived in Sodom." And Genesis 19:1 — he "sat in the gate of Sodom."

Brothers and sisters, four stages — and not one of them looks like an obvious fall. He never once made a decision that said, "I have decided to go bad." All he did, every single time, was choose whichever side looked the more reasonable.

And 2 Peter 2:7–8 calls him "righteous Lot, who was very distressed by the lustful life of the wicked", and says that this "righteous man dwelling among them was tormented in his righteous soul from day to day with seeing and hearing lawless deeds." So he was not numb. He was grieved. He simply did not leave.
Brothers and sisters, this is the part that stings: being grieved is not the same as being separated. You can be sorry about something and go on living in it for twenty years.
Why does the text make a point of telling us that "Lot sat in the gate of Sodom"?

The gate was where the ancient city held its councils and handed down its judgements — the man who sat there was an elder with a place of standing. So that one line reads like a curriculum vitae: he has arrived at the centre of that city. But set it beside the chapters that come before it, and what you see is a downward road. In chapter 13 he "traveled east" and "moved his tent as far as Sodom"; in chapter 14 he is the one "who lived in Sodom"; in chapter 19 he "sat in the gate." From a tent to a house, from the edge to the centre. And that is intensely practical for us: nobody walks into a place in a single day. He gets there by one small shift after another. So ask yourself the question at regular intervals — in the last six months, in which direction has the seat I sit in moved?
2 Peter calls Lot a "righteous" man, and yet nothing he does here looks righteous at all. How are we to understand that?

2 Peter 2:7–8 says that God "delivered righteous Lot, who was very distressed by the lustful life of the wicked", and that this "righteous man dwelling among them was tormented in his righteous soul from day to day with seeing and hearing lawless deeds." So Scripture's own verdict is this: the pain in him was real, and he did not agree with that city. Which gives us two lessons. First, a person can be grieved on the inside and still go on compromising, one step at a time, on the outside — grief is not the same thing as being set apart. Second, God's assessment is more generous than ours: even a man like this God calls righteous, and God comes personally to pull him out. So this chapter is not handing us a stick to beat Lot with. It is asking us to see ourselves in him.

In verses 2 and 3, Lot presses the two visitors hard to come into his house, because he knows exactly how dangerous that street becomes after dark. And what he sets before them is "unleavened bread", in Hebrew מַצּוֹת (*matsot*) — bread with no time to rise, the quickest bread there is. He is in a hurry.
Then verse 4: "But before they lay down, the men of the city, the men of Sodom, surrounded the house, both young and old, all the people from every quarter."

Brothers and sisters, in that one verse the writer piles up three separate phrases to nail the word "all" shut: the men of the city, both young and old, all the people from every quarter. Not one of them missing.

Verse 5: "Bring them out to us, that we may have sex with them." The Hebrew is וְנֵדְעָה אֹתָם, literally "that we may know them" — a euphemism, and what it points to here is the intent of a gang rape.

And then comes verse 8, the most shameful sentence in the whole chapter. Lot says, "See now, I have two virgin daughters. Please let me bring them out to you, and you may do to them what seems good to you."
Brothers and sisters, I am not going to defend that sentence — and neither does the text defend it.

Some will tell you that in that culture protecting the guest under your roof was the highest obligation there was, so what Lot faced was an impossible dilemma. That is an explanation; it is not a defence. Because look at what the text records next: his offer is not accepted. Instead the angels reach out, pull him inside the house, and protect the whole household with blindness. The human plan was set aside, and God's plan took its place.

And here is what I want you to see in that sentence. A father who is capable of saying such a thing is a father who has lived in that city far too long. An environment moves a person's line an inch at a time, and it keeps on moving it, until one day he hears himself say something he would never have believed he could say.

Brothers and sisters, this is the most practical warning the chapter gives us. You do not turn into another person all at once. You turn into one slowly. And the whole time it is happening slowly, you go on feeling like the same man you always were.
Lot hands his daughters over. Why does the text not condemn him outright?

Hebrew narrative very often withholds comment and lets the facts speak for themselves — and that is where its power lies. In fact the text has already passed its judgement through the structure. He begins by saying, "Please, my brothers, don't act so wickedly" — and the very next thing out of his mouth proposes another wickedness. He holds a seat in the gate, and yet not one person listens to a word he says; in verse 9 they answer, "This one fellow came in to live as a foreigner, and he appoints himself a judge." What this passage wants us to see is a father collapsing: his judgement, his authority and his household all give way in the same night. And we must say it very plainly: handing his daughters over was an indefensible evil. Scripture does not endorse it. Scripture is simply being honest about how bad a human being is capable of becoming.
3. A Light from the Original: the Hands That Took Hold of Them
In verse 12 the angels tell him to go and bring his family out. Verse 14 says he went and spoke to his sons-in-law — "But he seemed to his sons-in-law to be joking."

Brothers and sisters, that is a heavy sentence. Here is a man who has lived in that city for years, who sits in the gate and takes part in its councils — and on the one matter that mattered most, his own family thought he was making a joke. That is the price of the slow drift: at the moment your words are needed most, they carry no weight.
And then come verses 15 and 16, the heart of the whole chapter:
"When the morning came, then the angels hurried Lot, saying, 'Get up! Take your wife and your two daughters who are here, lest you be consumed in the iniquity of the city.' But he lingered."
Brothers and sisters — the fire is about to fall, the angels have already hurried him, and the man is still dawdling.
And then that same verse goes on: "the men grabbed his hand, his wife's hand, and his two daughters' hands, Yahweh being merciful to him; and they took him out, and set him outside of the city."
Count them: his hand, his wife's hand, his two daughters' hands — four hands. And there are only two angels doing the grabbing. Two hands each.
And the reason the text gives is not "because Lot deserved it." It is "Yahweh being merciful to him."
Brothers and sisters, this is the grace of the whole chapter. The reason he was saved is not that he was clearer-headed, or had more faith, or reacted faster than anybody else. He was pulled out.
In verse 17 the angel says three things: "Escape for your life! Don't look behind you, and don't stay anywhere in the plain. Escape to the mountains, lest you be consumed!"

Getting out is not enough. You may not look back, and you may not linger anywhere nearby either. Brothers and sisters, leaving something has three layers to it: your feet leave, your eyes leave, and your position leaves. Most people only ever manage the first.

And in verse 18 Lot's answer is — of all things — a negotiation: "Oh, not so, my lord." He begs to be allowed a little city instead of the mountain. And in verse 22 the angel says, "Hurry, escape there, for I can't do anything until you get there."
Brothers and sisters, weigh that sentence: the judgement of God is waiting for one man to reach a safe place. His hand cannot fall until that man has arrived.
"The angels hurried Lot … and the men grabbed his hand" — why did it have to be done by grabbing?

Because he lingered. Verse 16 states it without ornament: "But he lingered; and the men grabbed his hand, his wife's hand, and his two daughters' hands, Yahweh being merciful to him; and they took him out, and set him outside of the city." Four hands, and every one of them had to be taken hold of. And it is in this very verse that the word "merciful" appears — חָמַל (*chamal*). The mercy is God's; the merit is not Lot's. That is a deep comfort to us and a serious warning at the same time. The comfort is this: if you are standing today, it is very likely because somebody once took hold of your hand. The warning is this: delay really does cost something — on that night, his wife was one step behind.
If they had to be dragged out, where does a person's free will fit in?

This chapter does not cancel his freedom. The angels spoke first, hurried him first, gave him his chance first; it was he who lingered. And afterwards he still opened his mouth and asked, "Oh let me escape there" — and the angel granted it. So he was making decisions the whole way through. What has to be said is this: God's mercy will put out a hand, but when that hand comes, a person who keeps refusing to move will still meet the consequences. How God's sovereignty and human responsibility hold together is a long theological discussion, and these notes are not going to settle it from the pulpit. The practical posture is a good deal clearer: do what is yours to do — get up, walk — and leave the outcome with God. That is the shape Scripture keeps to throughout.
Verse 26: "But Lot's wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt."

Brothers and sisters, in English "looked back" can sound like nothing more than a flicker of curiosity. But the Hebrew verb here carries the sense of gazing, of lingering over the thing you are looking at — and the text says she was "from behind him". She had already fallen behind.
Her body was walking forward. Her heart was still in the city.
And in Luke 17:32 the Lord Jesus says just three words: "Remember Lot's wife!" When he is teaching about watchfulness at the end of the age, this is the example he reaches for.

Brothers and sisters, the Lord Jesus did not say, "Remember the fire of Sodom." He said, "Remember Lot's wife!" Which means the warning is not aimed at the people still inside the city. It is aimed at the people who have already come out.

Then in verses 27 and 28 the camera cuts back to the mountain: "Abraham went up early in the morning to the place where he had stood before Yahweh. He looked toward Sodom and Gomorrah, and toward all the land of the plain, and saw that the smoke of the land went up as the smoke of a furnace."
He had prayed his way down to ten and stopped there. The city did not have ten. He stands in the same spot as yesterday, and what he sees is smoke.

But verse 29 says something of the first importance: "When God destroyed the cities of the plain, God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the middle of the overthrow, when he overthrew the cities in which Lot lived."

Brothers and sisters, the text says it outright: the reason Lot was saved is that God remembered Abraham. That intercession did not save the city — but it saved a man. And from beginning to end, Lot never knew a thing about it.

As for what happens in the cave in verses 30 to 38, I do not intend to dwell on the detail, and the text itself is very restrained about it. It accounts for the origin of Moab and Ammon, the two nations Israel would be tangled up with for centuries afterwards. I will point out only one thing: a family that came out of Sodom carried Sodom out with them. A person can leave a city, and the city may not have left the person. And several hundred years later a Moabite woman named Ruth became the great-grandmother of David and entered the genealogy of the Lord Jesus himself. Out of the least presentable line in the whole book, God grafted in one of the brightest passages there is.
Lot's wife looks back once and becomes a pillar of salt. Is that punishment not far too heavy?

The Hebrew verb for "look" here is נָבַט (*nabat*), and it is more than the eye passing over something; it carries the sense of gazing, of lingering with longing. And she stopped to do it in the middle of running for her life. So this was not an absent-minded gesture. It was a heart that had never really left that city. As for the pillar of salt, the text records the fact and offers no explanation of the mechanism, and we do not need to invent one on its behalf. What deserves our attention is the use the Lord Jesus makes of it: in Luke 17:32 he says one sentence — "Remember Lot's wife!" — inside his teaching on watchfulness at the end of the age. So the point of this passage is not how severe the penalty was. The point is the question it puts to you: your feet have come out; what about your heart?
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot

The first, and the one I am going to say most forcefully: this chapter must never be used to shame or to attack a particular group of people. Scripture's indictment of Sodom is layered. Chapter 19 records a collective act of violence — the men of the whole city surrounding a house, intending to rape the visitors. Ezekiel 16:49 lists another layer: "pride, fullness of bread, and prosperous ease was in her and in her daughters. She also didn't strengthen the hand of the poor and needy." And Jude 7 says they gave themselves over to unnatural desire. Not one of those layers needs to be deleted, and not one of them may be added to. To flatten the whole chapter into a single charge and then aim that charge at a group of people is to turn the pulpit into a weapon. The test is very simple: when the congregation walks out, do they hold the justice of God in greater awe — or do they walk out with fresh grounds for looking down on somebody? And notice this: when the Lord Jesus mentions Sodom, he is rebuking the towns that saw his miracles and would not repent. He turns the camera back onto his own people.

The second is finding reasons for what Lot did when he pushed his daughters out of the door. That was the collapse of a father, and Scripture records it so that we can see how an environment warps a person's sense of right and wrong. If you defend him, you have quietly agreed that it is acceptable to trade one human being for another.

The third is preaching "looked back" as a small flicker of curiosity. Preach it lightly and the Lord's own sentence — "Remember Lot's wife!" — loses all its weight. She was not punished for a minor lapse. Her heart had never really left.

The fourth is preaching the fire of judgement and never reaching the hands that took hold. Those four hands in verse 16 are the grace of the chapter. If all you preach is the fire, what your congregation hears is intimidation. The last image of this sermon ought to be a pair of hands taking hold of somebody.

The fifth is taking the word "righteous" that 2 Peter uses of Lot and preaching it as though the man was really doing rather well. What Peter speaks of is his standing and the pain inside him, not his performance. 1 Corinthians 3:15 describes a kind of person who "will be saved, but as through fire" — saved, with the whole of his work burned away. Lot lost his wife, his household and his sons-in-law, and ended his days living in a cave. Salvation is free; delay has a price.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question. I am very uncomfortable in an environment — the way my company does things, the atmosphere in my extended family, a particular relationship — and I keep wanting to leave and keep not leaving. Am I simply Lot? Brothers and sisters, let me answer carefully. First: not every act of staying is delay. Daniel stayed in Babylon, Joseph stayed in Egypt, Esther stayed in the palace, and every one of them stayed in an ungodly environment and stood. So the question is not "where are you?" It is "who is that place turning you into?" Second, here are three very concrete checks. Has your line moved downward in the last two years? When you speak about your faith, do your family or your colleagues think you are joking? And the last time you grieved over that environment, did the grief simply pass — or did you actually do one thing about it? Third: if the answers make you uneasy, please do not decide on your own. Part of Lot's tragedy was that he was isolated — in that whole city there was not one person standing with him. Find a spiritual companion, and say this thing out loud.

The second question. There is someone in my family who will not listen no matter how I plead. Should I go on speaking? Brothers and sisters, this chapter gives us two very honest pictures. The first is the sons-in-law, to whom "he seemed … to be joking" — he pleaded, and it did no good at all. The second is verse 29: "God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the middle of the overthrow." The thing that actually worked was the man up on the mountain interceding for him — and Lot had no idea any of it was happening. So my advice is this: yes, keep speaking; but move the weight off persuading and onto interceding. You may well have said everything you have to say. You have not yet prayed everything you have to pray. And notice — Abraham prayed for a city, and God saved a man. God's answers very often do not look like our requests. But he answers.
My family is caught in a bad environment. How do I pull them out of it?

Start with that painful line in verse 14: Lot went and spoke to his sons-in-law, "But he seemed to his sons-in-law to be joking." A man who has been mixed up in that city for years finds that his words carry no weight. So the first thing is this: you have to be standing outside it yourself. Second, be concrete rather than merely reasonable — the angels took hold of hands; they did not argue anybody's mindset into shape. Third, accept that you will not be able to pull everyone out: Lot's sons-in-law never came out, and his wife looked back. What you can do is put your hand out, speak plainly, leave a road open, and then pray for them. And if that environment involves addiction, violence or fraud, you must seek professional help and go through the proper formal channels — do not rely on family persuasion alone.
7. Living 321 Out — the Whole Person Turns Round
Brothers and sisters, let us tie this lesson back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model — the angels took four hands and led a whole family out. And in Luke 22:32 the Lord Jesus says to Peter, "but I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn't fail." He prayed before Peter had fallen at all. Brothers and sisters, this is my role model: he puts his hand out first, and does not wait for me to steady myself.

The Bible is my standard — and in this chapter the standard is very short. It is the angel's three sentences: escape for your life, don't look behind you, don't stay anywhere in the plain. Brothers and sisters, sometimes a standard is not an elaborate set of principles. It is three simple actions. And our problem is usually not that we do not understand. It is that we do not do it.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — look carefully at the word in verse 15: the angels "hurried" Lot. There is a kind of guidance that is gentle, and there is a kind of guidance that hurries you. If lately you have kept being reminded of the same thing, kept being caught by the same verse, kept finding no settledness inside — that may not be you overthinking. That may be the hurrying.

Let Jesus be King — "Don't look behind you, and don't stay anywhere in the plain." Getting out is not enough; you may not go on circling the edges either. To let Jesus be King is for the whole person to turn round, leaving yourself not one angle from which to look back. Brothers and sisters, plenty of people have given a thing up and kept the app; have walked out of a relationship and kept the number. That is exactly what it means to stay in the plain.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — verse 16 says it plainly: "Yahweh being merciful to him." There is not one sentence of praise for Lot in the entire chapter. The whole reason he was saved is written into that one short phrase.

Establish God's system — verse 29: God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out. Brothers and sisters, one man's intercession saved another man. So to establish God's system means that there are people who go on standing up on the mountain for the people down in the city. If your church has a few older saints quietly keeping watch, treasure them — they are doing the work of verse 29.

And here I want to say something honest about 321 itself. We are fond of saying, "change the mindset and you change the life" — and Lot is a very good reminder from the other side, because his mindset was right. 2 Peter says his righteous soul was tormented day after day; that is to say, he could tell right from wrong, and the grief in him was genuine. And he did not move. So the sentence has to be finished properly: a mindset lit up by the Holy Spirit, plus the surrender of the will, plus practice and accountability inside a community — that is when a life actually changes. Mindset is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one. Lot knew. He simply did not leave.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, the Same Pair of Hands Taking Hold
Brothers and sisters, the same passage falls into four kinds of heart, and each of them sees something different.

The proud heart sees how depraved that city was. This heart finishes Genesis 19 more certain than ever of one thing: we are not like them. Brothers and sisters, notice where the text puts its weight — half the chapter is given over to describing how a "righteous man" lingered, how he bargained, how he lost his family. What the writer wants you to look at is not the people inside the city. It is the man who had to be dragged out of it.

The fearful heart sees the fire. This heart closes the chapter and begins to be afraid: is disaster going to come for me? Am I qualified to be pulled out? To that heart I want to say — look at the reason given in verse 16: "Yahweh being merciful to him." You were not taken hold of because your reactions were quick enough. And that line in verse 22, "I can't do anything until you get there", is the most comforting sentence in the chapter: the judgement is waiting for you to reach a safe place.

The ashamed heart sees its own delay. You may have been putting something off for years; every sermon reminds you, every time you fail to move, and you find it harder and harder to face God at all. Brothers and sisters, look at those hands. The angels did not stand in the doorway shouting, "Come out under your own steam." They walked in, and each of them took hold of two hands. God's way of dealing with delay is to reach out a hand, not to scold.

The wounded heart sees those two daughters. It may be that you really were pushed out of the door by your own family — used as a bargaining chip, required to be the one who was sacrificed, spent so that some adult could keep his face. Brothers and sisters, let me say this very clearly: Scripture wrote that down, and it does not say one good word for Lot. God does not stand on the side of the man who pushes somebody out. What God did was shut the door and protect that household with blindness. He saw the wound you carry, and in his own way he barred that door.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, write down the one thing you are currently delaying. Just one. You do not have to deal with it immediately; first move it from a vague feeling into a single sentence. Lot's problem was not that he did not know. It was that he never wrote it down and never set a date.

Second, check your three layers. Have your feet left? Have your eyes left? Has your position left? Find the one "angle to look back from" that you are still keeping — an app, a group chat, a phone number, a route you still drive — and deal with one of them this week.
Third, take the measure of your line. Think back to who you were two years ago: what was your standard on some particular matter? And now? If it has moved, in which direction has it moved?

Fourth, intercede for one "person in the city" for seven days. Pick somebody you have run out of ways to persuade, pray for him once a day this week, and stop arguing. The method of verse 29 is to stand up on the mountain.

Fifth, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church this week, in three sentences. The Bible records a city being destroyed, but the part that pierces is not the fire — it is three words: "But he lingered." He knew he ought to go, and he was genuinely grieved, and he did not move, and in the end he was dragged out with an angel holding his hand. And Scripture says the reason he was saved was not that his reactions were quick; it was that Yahweh was merciful to him.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that the reason I am saved is not that I was the clear-headed one; it is that a pair of hands could not bear to let me go.
I declare that my whole person will turn round, leaving myself not one angle from which to look back.
I declare that I will no longer let grief stand in for action; being sorry is not the same as being set apart.
I declare that for the people I can no longer persuade, I will stand up on the mountain and intercede.
This week I am to "check where I am sitting" — but I do not feel I have compromised on anything.

Use three very concrete questions. First, time: where has most of my time gone in the last six months? That place is shaping me. Second, language: whom does the way I talk lately sound more like than it did a year ago? People slowly pick up the tone of whatever surrounds them. Third, measure: is there something I would have thought improper three years ago and now think is perfectly all right? When exactly did that line move? And if no answer comes to mind, go and ask somebody who has known you a long time and is not afraid to tell you the truth. Lot's problem was not that he suddenly went bad. It was that he moved his tent one notch at a time, and nobody stopped him.
Brothers and sisters, if only one picture from this lesson may remain, let it be those four hands being taken hold of.

The morning has come. The angels are hurrying him. The fire is already on its way. And the man is still dawdling — he has a house in that city, and standing, and sons-in-law, and twenty years of a life. There is not one of them he can bear to part with.
And then the two messengers stop talking. They walk over, take two hands each, and drag four people out of the city.
The reason the text gives is one short phrase: "Yahweh being merciful to him."

Brothers and sisters, every one of us is saved in exactly this way. Not because our reactions were quick. Not because we were clearer-headed than the next person. Not because we made the right choice at the critical moment. There is One who could not bear it, and so he put out his hand.

And remember the man up on the mountain. Abraham went up early in the morning, stood in the place where he had stood the day before, and what he saw was smoke. From where he was standing, that intercession had failed — he had prayed his way down to ten, and not one of the ten could be found.
But verse 29 says: God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the middle of the overthrow.

He prayed for a city; God saved a person. What he could see was smoke; what God was doing was holding on to a hand. Your intercession for someone may be something nobody ever reports back to you — Lot went to his grave never knowing that somebody had stood for him that morning.

The focus is not on how long I have delayed, not on how bad that city was, and not on whether all I can see is smoke. The focus is on Jesus — the Lord who prays for us, and who reaches out with his own hand to pull us out. Not I, but Christ.

May God bless every one of us this week: to deal with one angle we could look back from, and to stand quietly on the mountain for one person we can no longer persuade. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the days of the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at a mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★★ From "traveled east" to "sat in the gate of Sodom" took several chapters. How does a person shift his way in, one step at a time?
2. ★★ 2 Peter calls Lot righteous and says he was tormented day after day. When someone is grieved inside and goes on staying anyway, where exactly does the problem lie?
3. ★ They came out with the angels "grabbing" their hands, and the reason given is "Yahweh being merciful to him." What does that show you?
4. ★★ The Lord Jesus uses one sentence only: "Remember Lot's wife!" What is it he wants to remind us of?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (I can go in and come out again whenever I like), fearful (if I leave, what is left of me?), ashamed (I am already in far too deep), wounded (an environment once destroyed me). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "the men grabbed his hand … Yahweh being merciful to him." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Is there something you would have thought improper three years ago and now think is perfectly all right? When exactly did that line move?
8. ★ Finish it in one sentence: "In the last six months, most of my time has gone to …"
9. ★★ This week, in which one matter will you refuse to linger — do it at once and stop putting it off? Say when, and say how.

Leader's reminder: question seven will touch compromises that are very hard to admit. The group leader should speak about his own first. Do not let members identify one another's, and do not press for details; if addiction, debt or anything unlawful is involved, follow up privately after the meeting and help them find formal and professional support.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ In your own home, is there someone who is drifting downward? What kind of hand will you put out to him this week?
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work or at school, is there a place you ought to be going to less often?

12. ★★★ The regular-review practice: this week give yourself the three-question check — where the time goes, whose voice you sound like, which line has moved. Say when you will do it, and who will look at it with you.
13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — and ask him to tell you honestly this week where he thinks you have changed. Say his name now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First: there is a man in the Bible who moved his tent towards a city one notch at a time, until he ended up sitting in that city's council chamber. Second: on the night that city was destroyed, he was dragged out with somebody holding on to his hand. Third: so I have learned to check at regular intervals where it is that I am sitting. Write down now who you will tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the one matter you will stop putting off this week, and the one person whose hand you will reach for. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord to be merciful to us, and to give us feet that are willing to get up at once.
